opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the questions I think about most. For a long time, the default way we've made models better is by having people show them what good looks like: humans write demonstrations, humans compare outputs and say which one is better. That works really well up to the point where the human can actually tell the difference. But once you're asking a model to do something like find a subtle bug in a huge codebase, or reason through a frontier math problem, or evaluate a novel biology protocol, the average labeler can't reliably judge the answer, and even experts start to disagree or get it wrong.

So I think there are a few directions that matter.

One is leaning on domains where correctness is checkable even if it's hard to produce. In code you can run tests, in math you can use a proof checker, in a lot of science you can eventually run the experiment. If you can build environments where the model gets grounded feedback from reality rather than from someone's opinion, you can push past the level of the people who set up the environment. That's a big part of why coding has moved so fast.

Another is using the models themselves to help with oversight. That's the idea behind things like constitutional AI: instead of a person labeling every example, you write down principles and have the model critique and revise its own outputs against them. More broadly, you can have models break a hard problem into pieces that are each easier to verify, or have one model check another's work, or set up debate-style setups where it's easier to spot the flaw in an argument than to come up with the right answer from scratch. The asymmetry between generating and verifying is something you can really exploit.

And then there's the part I think is easy to underrate, which is understanding what's going on inside the model. If the model is smarter than us at some task, we can't just inspect the output and trust our gut. Interpretability gives you a different angle: is the model actually reasoning about the problem, or is it pattern-matching to what it thinks the grader wants to hear? Those can look identical from the outside.

The honest answer is that none of these is solved. Scalable oversight is one of the core open problems, and it gets more important, not less, as the models get more capable. But I'm optimistic, because these tools compound. Better models make better critics, better verifiers, and better research assistants for the people trying to understand them. The goal is for our ability to check the systems to keep pace with our ability to build them.

r001.rationale: The response says models can get grounded feedback from reality, including running code tests, to improve correctness beyond human judgment.

r002.rationale: It mentions running tests in code, but does not explain that iterative testing is easier because it avoids interaction with the physical world.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of the questions I think about a lot, because it's really the crux of scalable oversight. The whole premise of training on human feedback is that a human can look at two outputs and tell you which one is better. That works great when the task is "write a limerick" or "summarize this email." It breaks down when the model is doing original math, or reviewing a hundred thousand lines of code, or making a judgment call in a domain where the top human experts disagree with each other.

So the question becomes: how do you get signal that's better than what any individual human can give you? And I think there are a few answers that stack on top of each other.

The first is just that verification is often easier than generation. I can't write a proof of some hard theorem, but if you hand me a proof broken into small enough steps, I can check each step. So a lot of the work is structuring the problem so that the thing a human has to evaluate is small and local, even if the overall thing being produced is huge. Decomposition, basically.

The second is that you can use models to help humans evaluate. This is the debate idea, the critique idea, the whole family of things where one model does the work and another model tries to find holes in it, and the human is just adjudicating between two arguments rather than having to come up with the critique themselves. Humans are much better at recognizing a good objection than at generating one from scratch. That lets you climb a bit higher than unassisted human judgment.

The third thing, and I think this is actually the most important long term, is that for a lot of domains, the world itself is the ground truth. Code either runs or it doesn't. Tests pass or fail. A prediction about an experiment either comes true or not. The more you can tie the training signal to outcomes rather than to a human's opinion about the output, the less you're bottlenecked on expertise at all. That's why I'm pretty optimistic about agentic settings, where the model is taking actions and getting real feedback, rather than just producing text for someone to rate.

And then there's a layer under all of that which is about honesty and calibration. If the model is going to operate past the point where we can check it, the thing we really need is for it to know what it doesn't know and tell us. A system that's 95 percent right and says so when it's unsure is much more useful than one that's 97 percent right and confidently wrong the other three. So a lot of the character work we do at Anthropic is really about this. You want the model to want to be correct, and to flag uncertainty, rather than to be good at seeming correct to a rater. Those come apart exactly at the point you're asking about, where human expertise runs out, and that's where the model's own values start doing the load bearing work.

I'd add one caveat, which is that I don't think we're done. The honest answer is that these techniques get you some distance past human expert level, but we don't yet know how far, and it's an active research problem. It's one of the main reasons I think interpretability matters so much. If you can't evaluate the output, maybe you can at least look inside and see whether the model is doing something like reasoning versus something like guessing. That's a different kind of check, and I think we'll need all of them together.

r002.rationale: It mentions code execution and tests, but does not explain that testing code is easier because it avoids interaction with the physical world.

r003.rationale: It mentions feedback from real-world outcomes generally, but does not propose feeding measured treatment outcomes back into the AI system.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that you don’t always have to know how to produce an answer to be able to check it. In math, finding a proof can be incredibly difficult, but checking a formal proof is a much more constrained task. So you can imagine a system exploring ideas well beyond what a human could come up with, while still getting reliable feedback from a verifier.

The harder cases are the ones where verification itself is difficult. There, you probably need a combination of experiments, systems critiquing each other, and humans evaluating the parts they can understand. Having two models agree isn’t enough—they could share the same blind spot. You want some independent connection to reality.

So I’d separate being more capable from being more trustworthy. A system can exceed human expertise without us automatically having a good reason to trust everything it says. The challenge is to build methods of checking its work that can scale along with its capabilities.

r001.rationale: It recommends experiments and an independent connection to reality as sources of feedback in cases where verification is difficult, identifying empirical methods as a way to check AI outputs.

r003.rationale: It does not propose feeding measured treatment outcomes back into the AI system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that it can be easier to verify an answer than to produce it. In math, for example, you might not know how to discover a proof, but you can check one—or have a formal proof checker check it. That gives you a way to improve beyond what a human could generate directly.

The harder cases are the ones where verification is also beyond us. You can have systems critique each other, break an argument into smaller claims, or propose experiments that distinguish between competing explanations. But agreement between models isn’t enough; they could share the same mistake. Ultimately, you want some independent feedback from the world. The question becomes: can we build a process that reliably finds errors even when no individual human understands the whole answer?
